article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Balanced hybrid
Genetics: Undisclosed proprietary hybrid
Breeder: Paradise Seeds
THC Content: 15–20%
CBD Content: Low, generally below 1%
Terpene Profile: myrcene , caryophyllene , limonene
Primary Flavors: Creamy fruit, grape, tropical fruit punch
Flowering Time (Indoor): 55–60 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: Early to mid-October
Indoor Yield: Approximately 450 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Approximately 600–1,000 g per plant
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Opium is a cannabis strain whose dramatic name is matched by an unusually rich combination of flavor, resin production, and balanced effects. Paradise Seeds spent several generations developing this cultivar from what the breeder describes only as “original classic lines,” deliberately keeping the precise parentage private. What emerged was a 50/50 indica-sativa marijuana hybrid capable of producing thick stems, heavy trichome-covered flowers, and a surprisingly creamy fruit flavor that contrasts with its powerful cerebral onset.

Opium also earned major recognition shortly after its release, placing second in the Sativa Cup at the 2006 High Times Cannabis Cup in Amsterdam. With a manageable flowering period of roughly 60 days, indoor yields around 450 grams per square meter, and considerably larger plants outdoors, it combines connoisseur-quality flower with enough production potential to interest serious growers. Its appeal is ultimately broader than potency alone: this is old-school European weed breeding built around structure, aroma, resin, and a high that moves smoothly between mental stimulation and physical calm.
Genetics and Lineage

Paradise Seeds has never publicly disclosed the exact parents of Opium. The breeder instead explains that the cultivar was developed over several generations using genetics from established classic cannabis lines. The finished plant is classified as an even 50% sativa and 50% indica hybrid. That makes claims assigning Opium a specific named two-parent pedigree difficult to support. Some modern descriptions characterize the ancestry broadly as old landrace-derived or proprietary genetics, but the most accurate reference-page treatment is simply that the lineage remains breeder-protected.

What can be learned from the plant itself is more informative than speculative parent names. Opium has the thick stem, bushy lateral branching, dense flower formation, and relatively quick maturation commonly associated with indica-influenced cannabis , yet its outdoor growth can become surprisingly tall and tree-like in warm climates. The effects also reveal the hybrid nature clearly: an immediate cerebral lift reflects the sativa side, while the indica component provides enough physical depth to keep that mental intensity from disappearing quickly. Paradise Seeds specifically describes this combination as a fast “take-off” supported by an indica influence that carries the experience through its later stages.
Effects and Experience

Opium tends to begin quickly and mentally. The first portion of the high can feel vivid, uplifting, and strongly cerebral, with sensory perception becoming more noticeable and ordinary entertainment taking on additional intensity. Paradise Seeds historically characterized the experience as visual, cerebral, and powerful. Music, movies, creative hobbies, and relaxed exploration can fit this phase particularly well. Unlike a heavy indica that announces itself primarily through body weight, Opium initially feels more expansive and mentally engaging.

Physical relaxation gradually develops underneath that energetic start. The indica half of the genetics creates a steadier landing, softening muscular tension and preventing the experience from feeling purely racy. At moderate doses, this balance can remain comfortable and functional; heavier consumption is more likely to create mental haze and stronger physical relaxation. Historical grow reports also characterize the effects as strong and long-lasting. Because reported THC levels commonly fall around 15–20% and can reach somewhat higher in optimized modern crops, inexperienced consumers should still approach the cultivar conservatively.
Medical Benefits

Medical marijuana consumers may find the combination of cerebral elevation and physical relaxation appealing when they want something less sedating than a traditional indica. Cannabis with this style of effect is sometimes chosen when temporary stress, low mood, appetite changes, or general physical tension are concerns. The relatively bright beginning may allow some consumers to remain engaged with normal activities before the heavier portion of the experience develops.

Opium itself has not been established in controlled clinical trials as a treatment for pain, depression, anxiety, insomnia, or any other specific medical disorder. Its chemistry also cannot be predicted solely from the strain name, especially because phenotype and cultivation conditions can influence THC, CBD, and terpene production. Higher doses of THC may cause anxiety, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, or impaired coordination in sensitive consumers. Anyone using weed medically should therefore consider laboratory results for the actual flower and appropriate professional healthcare guidance.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Fruit dominates the aromatic profile, but Opium does not smell like a simple modern candy strain. Paradise Seeds describes fruit as the primary fragrance and creaminess as a defining element of the finished taste. Cured flowers may suggest grape, tropical fruit punch, citrus peel, and ripe mixed fruit over a warmer background of earth and spice. Breaking apart the dense buds can release stronger pungency, creating a contrast between the sweet surface aroma and more traditional cannabis depth underneath.

The creamy character becomes especially noticeable on the inhale, where fruit sweetness can develop an almost cocktail-like richness. Grape and citrus often appear toward the front, followed by earthy herbs and mild spice on the finish. Modern descriptions commonly associate the cultivar with myrcene, caryophyllene, limonene, and pinene, although Paradise Seeds does not publish a standardized terpene fingerprint for every plant. As with any seed-grown marijuana cultivar, phenotype, lighting, harvest timing, drying, and curing can shift the final aromatic balance considerably.
Growing Information

Opium develops a strong central framework with a thick main stem and vigorous bushy side branches. Paradise Seeds specifically emphasizes this structure because it gives the plant enough strength to carry unusually large and heavy flowers. Indoors, the cultivar can be grown as a larger multi-branched specimen or placed into a Sea of Green arrangement. It responds well to training, and historical breeder information notes particularly impressive performance in hydroponic systems. Flowering takes approximately 55–60 days, while indoor production is typically listed at about 450 grams per square meter.

Resin formation becomes increasingly obvious as flowering advances. Mature buds grow thick, compact, and heavily coated with trichomes, producing a high flower-to-leaf ratio that makes the strain visually impressive and relatively efficient to trim. The weight of the colas can become substantial, so branch support may be useful in high-performing gardens. Maintaining airflow is equally important because exceptionally dense flowers create areas where moisture can become trapped late in bloom.

Outdoors, Opium changes character dramatically. Paradise Seeds describes plants in warm, sunny regions such as southern France, Spain, and California as becoming more tree-like than bush-like. Harvest generally arrives in early to mid-October. Outdoor yield figures vary between surviving breeder-derived listings, from approximately 600 grams to as much as 1,000 grams per plant under ideal conditions. Northern growers should be more cautious: the same oversized, dense flowers that make Opium productive can become vulnerable when cool autumn weather brings persistent rain and humidity.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Opium?

Paradise Seeds has never publicly disclosed the exact parents. The breeder states that Opium was developed over several generations from original classic cannabis lines and classifies the finished strain as an even 50% sativa and 50% indica hybrid.
Is Opium indica or sativa?

Opium is a balanced hybrid containing approximately equal indica and sativa influence. Its growth shows dense, sturdy indica-style flower development, while the effects begin with a strong cerebral character before gradually becoming more physically relaxing.
What does the Opium strain taste like?

Sweet and creamy fruit forms the core flavor. Grape, tropical fruit punch, citrus, earth, and mild spice may appear around that foundation. Paradise Seeds specifically emphasizes a fruity fragrance and creamy taste.
How long does Opium take to flower?
Indoor plants generally require approximately 55–60 days of flowering. Outdoor crops typically mature in early to mid-October in the Northern Hemisphere.
Did Opium win a Cannabis Cup?

Opium placed second in the Sativa category at the 2006 High Times Cannabis Cup in Amsterdam. It also received recognition at the 2006 IC 420 Growers Cup, helping establish the cultivar’s reputation shortly after its introduction.
Final Thoughts on Opium

Opium demonstrates why a breeder does not need to disclose every parent for a cannabis strain to develop a recognizable identity. Paradise Seeds spent several generations refining the plant, eventually producing a balanced hybrid with thick stems, bushy growth, oversized resinous flowers, creamy fruit flavor, and a cerebral high that gradually gains physical weight. Its 2006 competition success further established the genetics during an influential period in European marijuana breeding.

For growers, the strain combines a relatively efficient 55–60-day indoor flowering period with approximately 450 g/m² production and much larger outdoor potential in sunny climates. For consumers, the attraction lies in the contrast between tropical fruit and creamy sweetness on one side and a strong, long-lasting head-and-body experience on the other. Opium remains a distinctive Paradise Seeds cultivar precisely because it balances so many characteristics without leaning completely toward either indica or sativa—a productive, resin-heavy hybrid with enough old-school personality to remain recognizable decades after its introduction.
